title: Concatenate and align
goal: Combine rows or columns while respecting index labels.
prerequisites: Understand DataFrame indexes and missing values.

cells.title: Stack row batches
cells.explanation: concat stacks tables when axis=0, the default. ignore_index=True assigns new position labels. This changes the index, not the Student_ID values.
cells.code:
df = students()
first = df.iloc[:6]
second = df.iloc[6:]
result = pd.concat([first, second], ignore_index=True)
print(result[["Student_ID", "Name"]])

questions.prompt: What is the list inside concat?
questions.answer: It contains the two DataFrames to combine.

questions.prompt: How many student rows will result have?

questions.answer: No. It only creates a fresh integer index; duplicate data would still remain.

cells.task: Stack the second batch before the first, and reset the index in the combined result.
cells.hint: Reverse the order of the two DataFrames passed to concat.
cells.solution:
df = students()
result = pd.concat([df.iloc[6:], df.iloc[:6]], ignore_index=True)
print(result[["Student_ID", "Name"]])
cells.solution_note: S007 is first because concat keeps the order of the input batches.

check.feedback: A fresh range index is assigned; data values stay unchanged.

cells.watch: Build a list of batches and concatenate once instead of repeatedly growing a DataFrame in a loop.
cells.takeaway: Use concat for batches with the same meaning and schema.

cells.title: Align columns by labels
cells.explanation: concat with axis=1 places objects side by side. It matches index labels, even when their order differs. This is why an ID index is safer than assuming row positions match.
cells.code:
names = pd.Series(["Amira", "Bilal"], index=["S001", "S002"], name="Name")
scores = pd.Series([72, 88], index=["S002", "S001"], name="Score")
result = pd.concat([names, scores], axis=1)
print(result)

questions.prompt: Why are the two Series given names?
questions.answer: Their names become output column labels.
88, because both values use index label S001.

questions.prompt: Why is assigning scores.to_numpy() risky here?
questions.answer: It discards labels, so the first score, 72, would be assigned by position to Amira.

cells.task: Add score 91 for S003, then concatenate using join="inner" so only shared IDs remain.
cells.hint: Construct a three-value scores Series and set join="inner".
cells.solution:
names = pd.Series(["Amira", "Bilal"], index=["S001", "S002"], name="Name")
scores = pd.Series([72, 88, 91], index=["S002", "S001", "S003"], name="Score")
result = pd.concat([names, scores], axis=1, join="inner")
print(result)
cells.solution_note: S003 is excluded because its label is absent from names.

check.prompt: What does axis=1 concatenate side by side?
check.feedback: Column concatenation aligns the row indexes.

cells.watch: Resetting indexes before concatenating unrelated tables can hide a mismatched-key problem.
cells.takeaway: Alignment follows labels, not visual row order.

cells.title: Request a specific index order
cells.explanation: reindex requests specific labels in a specific order. A requested label that does not exist produces missing values. It can also omit existing labels that were not requested.

questions.answer: The label list supplied to reindex.
Missing Name and Score values because the ID does not exist.

questions.prompt: How is this different from loc with a missing label?
questions.answer: With a list of IDs, loc raises KeyError if any requested ID is absent. reindex can create rows with missing values for absent labels. Label slices have different endpoint rules.

cells.task: Reindex to S012, S002, S001 and print the Name and Score columns in that order.
cells.hint: Supply a different list of labels to reindex.
cells.solution_note: All three labels exist, so this result has no missing values.

check.prompt: What does an absent label create during reindex?
options: A copy of the preceding row
check.feedback: reindex creates missing entries for labels not present in the original unique index.

cells.watch: Reindexing generally requires unique labels on the axis being reindexed.
cells.takeaway: Reindex is an explicit request for labels and order.

cells.title: Fill from a second source
cells.explanation: combine_first fills missing values from matching labels in another object. Existing non-missing values in the first source win. Agree which source has priority before applying this rule.
cells.code:
primary = pd.Series([88, pd.NA, 91], index=["S001", "S002", "S003"], dtype="Int64")
backup = pd.Series([85, 72, 90], index=["S001", "S002", "S003"], dtype="Int64")
result = primary.combine_first(backup)
print(result)

questions.answer: primary, because combine_first is called on it.
No. Its primary score 88 is already present.

questions.prompt: Why is this different from an unconditional overwrite?
questions.answer: Only missing primary entries are filled; existing values remain.

cells.task: Reverse the source priority by calling combine_first on backup. Explain the S001 result.
cells.solution:
primary = pd.Series([88, pd.NA, 91], index=["S001", "S002", "S003"], dtype="Int64")
backup = pd.Series([85, 72, 90], index=["S001", "S002", "S003"], dtype="Int64")
result = backup.combine_first(primary)
print(result)
cells.solution_note: Backup now wins wherever it has a value; S001 is 85.

check.prompt: Which primary values are replaced by combine_first?
options: Only missing values with an available backup
check.feedback: Existing primary values are retained, including legitimate zero values.

cells.watch: An unmatched backup label can expand the index; inspect the result size.
cells.takeaway: Filling from another source is a policy as well as a method.
